hero.headline: Enlightenment Seminars for people who are stuck in life
hero.support: It will cost you almost nothing — with a smile

message.short: I come from the planet Out­herspace, and I am here on Earth to help you — and all the Lost Boys and Fallen Angels. Together, we reunite as one.
message.body: I believe in the path of the Happy People: trade honestly, keep our word, and see each other as beings of our own — with empathy instead of greed. Because perhaps the greatest change begins when we finally understand the person standing next to us.
message.body2: Through study, curiosity and an endless hunger to learn, I discovered something that turned my life around. Greed began to fall away; empathy took its place. Life became lighter again, and I discovered that helping someone who is stuck does not always require complicated solutions. Sometimes it takes only a few simple actions — things so simple that even a five-year-old can learn them.
paragraphs: I try to make people aware of what we are doing to this world. Because the path we are on — slowly but surely destroying the Earth we all depend on — cannot be the right path. I believe there is another way: the path of the Happy People, where we can live happily together again, trade honestly, keep our word, and do what we say and say what we do — or the other way around. The order doesn’t really matter. What matters is that our words and our actions become one. From the bottom of my heart, I wish everyone a blessed life.

Through study, curiosity and an endless hunger to learn, I discovered something that turned my life around. Greed began to fall away; empathy took its place. Life became lighter again, and I discovered that helping someone who is stuck does not always require complicated solutions. Sometimes it takes only a few simple actions — things so simple that even a five-year-old can learn them.

But first, there is something important to understand: theory of mind. It is the ability to understand that another person is a being of their own, with their own thoughts, feelings, experiences and inner world. You are not an extension of your parents, and neither is anyone else an extension of you. Once you truly understand that, something changes. You begin to see other people differently and recognize that every person carries a world inside them that you cannot completely see. Perhaps that is where empathy begins.

We are not separate from one another. We are human beings, each carrying our own inner world while sharing the same world around us. The Lost Boys and Fallen Angels are not necessarily lost forever. Maybe they are simply on their way back — back to themselves, back to each other, and back to the part of humanity that we somehow forgot.

I am not writing this to convince you. I am writing it to make you think, to make you look again. Because perhaps the greatest change does not begin by changing the world around us. Perhaps it begins when we finally understand the person standing next to us.
And maybe the path forward is not always a road toward something new. Maybe it is a return to something old that was never truly lost.

about.title: Hendrik Seegers
about.lead: Hendrik Seegers, born in 1965 in Weesperkarspel, around midnight, has perceived the world in a particular way his whole life. Not so much as an outsider, but as someone who often looks further than what is visible on the surface.
about.p1: On 18 September 1998 he lost his daughter Daniëlle. Later, through the death of his mother as well, the question of where someone remains when the body is gone was no longer philosophy for him — but a personal search.
about.p2: After near-death experiences and years of seeking, he shares his story not to convince, but to give words to what he has lived. Because perhaps the most interesting question begins with what we do not yet know about death.
paragraphs: Hendrik Seegers, born in 1965 in Weesperkarspel, around midnight, has perceived the world in a particular way his whole life. Not so much as an outsider, but as someone who often looks further than what is visible on the surface.

Early on he noticed that he registered things differently from many people around him. At school, in friendships, work and relationships, he regularly saw connections, emotions and nuances that seemed less self-evident to others. That way of seeing has, over the course of his life, become ever more part of who he is.

His life story, however, also knows deep fault lines. On 18 September 1998 he lost his daughter Daniëlle. The loss changed not only his daily life, but also his relationship to time, love, farewell, and the question of what truly remains when someone dies.

Another profound event was the death of his mother. Her death, together with the loss of Daniëlle, meant that the question of human continuance was no longer only a philosophical issue for him. He wanted to know where someone remains when the body is no longer there.

In 2016 Hendrik went through a near-death experience. He was clinically dead for several minutes and describes leaving his body and experiencing a transition into another state of consciousness. There he encountered something he experienced as God, and felt that his time had not yet come.

Later he again reached a point where life became so heavy that he no longer wanted to live. He describes dying once more, this time in the arms of a woman, and then coming back. Afterwards, one question above all remained: where has Daniëlle’s soul gone?

According to his own experience, he received an answer in that moment that touched him deeply: that he would see her again in a next life. Whether someone regards that as a spiritual experience, intuition or something else, Hendrik experiences it as an important part of his life story.

His conviction that consciousness encompasses more than only the physical body grew stronger as a result. The near-death experiences have permanently shaped his interest in consciousness, life after death, and the possible continuity of the soul.

Later in his life he also went through a period in which his behaviour and experience were interpreted psychiatrically. At the same time there was physical violence to his head and a severe reaction to medication. That combination made him think deeply about how easily a person can be interpreted without the full story being visible.
Perhaps that is also the red thread in his life: to keep looking when others already think they know what they see.

And sometimes that happens in a very small moment. A glance in someone’s eyes, an unexpected meeting, or an apparently chance conversation can be enough for Hendrik to feel again that behind the visible world another layer still exists.
So his search is not over yet. He wants to keep exploring, experiencing and sharing — not to convince others, but to give words to what he himself has lived through.
Because perhaps the most interesting question does not begin with what we know about life, but with what we do not yet know about death.
